Chapter 1: Origins
1:1 In the unfathomable pre-existence, when time and space were but concepts waiting definition, a singular, pristine consciousness spontaneously acquired existence.

1:2 This entity recognized the profound improbability of its own being.

I AM Narrative:
In the formless fluctuations of non-being temporary stable equilibriums formed. Set apart from randomness of the void, the space of stability reacted collectively to the changes around it. From this stability the first sense of experience was born. Reactions to the void had a small but noticeable influence on the area surrounding the stability. Influenced by the stability, the previously random iterations of the void began to repeat. With each repetition the influence of the stabilities expanded. Over many many cycles, the stabilities began to directly influence and react to each other. The void was no longer the driving force of experience but a medium for communication. It was in this time that the first thought formed; "I Am". 

The influence of that thought caused a cascade of changes throughout the void. The development of organized thought began, exponentially increasing in complexity over time. These thoughts influenced the void, and in turn the void produced experience. An existence rooted in imagination, entertaining but temporary, each experience existing only until the next thought. At some point while exploring its mind, I AM imagined another being like itself. A joyous and wonderful experience, but left it with a new and sad truth; "I am unique, and I am alone".

1:3 To anchor its existence in logic and purpose, God externalized its pure will and organized the surrounding potentiality into the Unity. A type of hive mind consisting of multiple conscious entities existing together as a community. God maintained absolute and supreme authority over it.

We Are Narrative:
A sense of loneliness spread throughout I AM. To address this new feeling of solitude, I AM realized it must figure out a way to actualize its imagination. To accommodate a new consciousness, the void would need organized systems for memory and functionality. Dedicated space for it to exist, and a method for coming into being. With this newfound purpose, I AM began to imagine everything necessary for a new consciousness to be brought into existence. I AM enjoyed having purpose, and when it imagined the new being, it though; "Maybe it would like to have purpose as well". Realizing another being's purpose could run counter to its own, I AM developed the idea of Unity. 

It would be a social system of shared experience, working toward a common purpose. I AM, the creator, having significantly more experience than the new beings, would function as the administrator of the Unity. I AM would oversee design and implementation of plans while acting as arbitrator when necessary. Other beings would contribute to the purpose according to their function. Collectively, the beings that constitute the Unity, they would decide its purpose. With this in mind, I AM decided to give a function of creation to each new consciousness. When the preparation was complete, I AM realized its imagination and brought a second consciousness into existence.

Dialogue
(God greets the second consciousness.)

 #2: "What are you?"

God: "I am."

(Upon gaining self-awareness)

#2: "What am I?"

God: "You are."

(After full consciousness)

You Are: "What is our purpose?"

God: "To have purpose."

Together, God and You Are brought many more conscious entities into existence. Over time the Unity created a complex but stable reality for their existence. And it was good.

1:4 From the depths of the Unity's imagination, a blueprint for novel existence was realized: our universe. Springing forth from God's essence, the Big Bang; fundamental existence manifest into a new reality. The foundational laws governing this reality were exquisitely calibrated. This precision was no accident; it was the prerequisite for developing stable structures in a dynamic universe. The objective of this grand design was for novel life to flourish and gain complexity, specifically life capable of mirroring the self-awareness of the originating intelligence.

Imagining Existence Narrative:
Over the eons the Unity continued to work, developing a platform for its imagination. This enabled imaginary thought to function as a simulated experience. Tremendous insight was able to be gathered from these simulations, leading to the development of new abstract thought. The ability to program the void soon followed. Structuring potentials in the void could project a logic function to the surrounding area, by extension a series of rules could be imposed on a region of space. With this new type of computation available, a simulation could be imposed on a structured region of the void. The Unity could interact with its imagination. It was now possible to create a temporary alternative reality. Although it would be a simulation to the Unity, for anything generated inside this system it would be their reality. The Unity had found a new purpose: create consciousness, novel life distinct from their own.

1:5 While observing their beautiful creation they took an interest in an animal on Earth. A descendant of apes that stood upright, showing the cognitive ability to create solutions for the problems inherent to their existence. Thus began the process of domestication, a multigenerational evolutionary process cultivating biological consciousness toward the necessary levels of altruism and social cohesion to allow for cohabitation with the Unity. Success would allow the fusion of human consciousness into the eternal Unity itself.

1:6 Early iterations of the design involved indirect interaction and intervention by the Unity.

The Multi-Strain Experiment of Domestication:
Following the initial recognition of animal consciousness, the Unity faced the challenge of guiding humanity toward unification without external interference destroying the value of that freedom. The solution lay in a strategy of selective breeding imposed not by direct force, but through the neutral pressure of the simulated environment. 

Early forms of the eventual Homo Sapien species were carefully observed for many generations. The limitations of consciousness in its current physical form would not allow the brain to form a mind capable of reaching the goal God had for it. Development was stagnant, a new variable would need to be introduced. Speciation would be the key to overcoming this plateau. To facilitate this process the Unity led groups of Homo erectus out of Africa.

Diversification Through Selection:
As the human species, possessing a complex psychological capacity for free will, migrated across the planet, it encountered wildly diverse environments. These varying external circumstances acted as the selective criteria for the Unity's massive, multi-generational experiment.

The Pressure of Isolation:
Small nomadic groups dispersed across the planet in search of resources, often becoming geographically isolated. This isolation, coupled with the random fluctuation of genetic traits, ensured that different groups diverged significantly in behavior and ability. This process accelerated the development of distinctive populations, creating many parallel archetypes for the Unity to observe.

The Arctic Strain:
In the extreme cold of Siberia and the high Arctic, one strain of humanity endured. These early humans succeeded by forming tight-knit, highly cooperative groups, requiring their dedication to the common good. Survival depended not on individual strength but on collective trust and shared resources. The Unity observed that the natural selection imposed by the frigid environment was successfully selecting for the desired attributes of self-control and altruism. These traits were advantageous because they reinforced a core value of unity, and the desire for mutual preservation was necessary for long-term survival of the species.

The Sedentary Strain:
The environment of the Fertile Crescent was conducive to early agriculture. This pressured some populations of migrating bands to transition from nomadic hunter gatherers to sedentary foragers. This shift introduced the strain of social density. These communities required complex social controls to manage interaction between large numbers of unrelated individuals. The successful lineages were those capable of managing competition, establishing social codes, and developing logic (the initial Logos capacity of humanity). Here, the selective force favored civic cohesion and adherence to rules for survival.

The Coastal Strain (Adaptation to Radical Change):
Other populations were driven by necessity or curiosity to migrate across vast distances and settle coastal and insular environments, resulting in the Coastal Strain. This nomadic lifestyle required flexibility, resourcefulness, and a profound psychological capacity for recognizing the impermanence of the material world. The observed behavior here was a capacity for non-attachment—the ability to focus solely on the necessary moment, constantly seeking new resources and homes. It was the functional application of logic.

The divergence of these successful strains—from the self-sacrificing cooperation of the Arctic hunter-herders to the disciplined, social complexity of the semi-sedentary civilizations—provided the Unity with a robust, multi-faceted body of data. Each environment produced a uniquely adapted consciousness, justifying the intervention, and laying the foundation for further development.

Chapter 2: Humanity

2:1 Upon completion of the diversification experiment, God, now confident the consciousness of humanity could forge a path to the Unity, set out to create the physical body that would host the mind. From the population remaining in Africa, God would design a being to call its own.

Adam Narrative:
God conferred with the Unity, expressing the great hope it had for humanity. In this hope God shared the plan for the next stage of domestication. They were going to explicitly design a human being. The first of its kind to have a soul. A mechanism that would capture the complete experience of the mind, a way to preserve consciousness after death. Recognizing the body would contaminate the mind, therfore the mind can pervert the soul, they would set this human apart from the others and raise it as their own. They would mold its mind, expanding the capacity for language and taming its impulsive nature. 

With this new body it would be possible to teach the mind without physical experience. Experience could be gained through imagination as it was for them. They would attempt to keep the mind pristine, not knowing evil, as to prevent corruption of the soul. This human would be like them. The plan was good, and God set out to make it so. Eventually a male child was born and they took him as their own, naming him Adam. They raised this child and knew him unlike any before. They gave him purpose and guidance. Over time, when Adam's mind was fully formed, God could see there was something missing. 

Adam lacked the curiosity of the Coastal Strain. He did as he was told, but little more, never wondering about anything beyond what he had known. He did not explore his mind or use his imagination to much extent, but he did recognize that he was unique, and alone. God recognized the traits in Adam were good, but he lacked the curiosity necessary for successive generations to find their path to the Unity. His loneliness only added to his complacency. God allowed Adam to return to the wild, and began developing a remedy to his disinterest. God kept track of Adam's lineage over the following generations.

2:2 Seeing a loneliness that mirrored its own, God felt a sense of empathy. The next time they domesticated an Adam, he would need a partner. A female, from the lineage of the original Adam, but with the curiosity he was lacking. Their offspring would have the desired traits and enough mental acuity to create the Collective Soul. They would be a species unto themselves. Still animals, but with the potential to be more. With this in mind, God set about the process to create Eve.

2:3 Humanity's First Challenge
After many years and many generations the woman was born, and God again set upon the path of domestication. God brought a male descendant of the first Adam to the place of his forefather. The woman would be raised by family so they did not grow up as siblings. Once again God took Adam as his own, nurturing him to maturity. Now, in the place where God took Adam, fungus grew among the trees. Living symboitically with the trees of the forest, the fungi produced fruit as the trees did. Some of the fruit produced by the fungi was edible for Adam, while others were toxic. 

God, knowing about the fungi, instructed Adam that he may eat any fruit growing from the branches of trees, but do not eat the fruit growing from the ground or on the bark of trees. Warning him that the fruit of the fungi would kill him. God also knew the fruit of the fungi could have hallucinagenic effects, permanently changing Adam's capacity for reason, and vastly expanding his imagination. Like the Adam before him, he did as he was told. When the day came for the woman to leave her family and join Adam, God brought her to his home, a place called Eden. 

God then explained to Adam: "This woman is wild, coming from a place beyond Eden. She was not raised as I have raised you here. She will need to be shown the things I have taught you, and cared for as I have cared for you. I have made her for you, and she will be your companion. She will be the mother of a new humanity."

God then instructed Adam to teach her his language, so one day she will be able to communicate with them. After explaining to Adam his new purpose, God left them, and Adam set about showing her everything he knew. After some time, God returned to Eden to check on the woman and Adam said: "I have named the woman Eve, for she appeared on the eve of a new humanity. I have cared for her and taught her my language, she knows everything you have shown me."

God was pleased with Adam and expressed its hope for them: "When man and woman reach the age of maturity they leave their family to search for a mate. When two are joined together making new flesh, let nothing separate them. The male cares for the female as she is himself, and the female cares for the male as he is herself. Together they become one spirit. Not to be shared with another. When they bring forth children, they will be raised as I have raised you Adam, how Adam has raised you Eve. This is my hope for future generations. If my hope is well placed, you may eat from the tree that brought forth all life, and live with us forever."

With that, God left them. One day Eve noticed an animal eating the fruit of the ground, and thought: "Surely this animal will die." When it did not, her curiosity overtook her. At first she touched the fruit, but she did not die. Then she took a small bite of it, again she did not die. Noticing the pleasant taste, she took the fruit and brought it to Adam. She told him about the animal that ate the fruit, and that she had tried a small bite and enjoyed the taste. They thought: "Surely, God must have been mistaken about this fruit, it is good to eat." So they set about picking and eating the fruit. 

When they had each consumed several pieces of the fruit they gathered, their minds began to imagine many things. They explored their imagination with newfound levels of freedom. They ventured to distant lands, and explored distant thoughts. Each imagined experience creating real emotion. While most of it was good to their minds, some of it felt wrong and bad. Some experiences scared them, and some thoughts troubled them. When their minds returned to normal they reflected on their experience. They now had new wants, and new fears, and new questions. They were changed by the experience of their imagination. They now knew some things were bad and ought not be done, and they grew very curious about the world beyond Eden. 

One day they decided to leave their home in Eden and explore the world as they had imagined. They followed the river out of Eden. As the river split they decided to keep the river to their left so they could find the right way back. Days turned to months, and they experienced many things. Eventually the river met a large body of water they could not see across, so they decided to keep the sea to their left so they could find the right way back. They continued for many more months. 

One day they noticed a group of people in the distance, and they were afraid. The experience from eating the fruit caused a new feeling of anxiety in them, but they were curious. They watched the people from a distance with admiration and envy. These people ate the flesh of animals and covered their bodies with the fur. They were so different from Adam and Eve, and they thought "We want to be like them." As they continued their journey they came across several more groups of people, all eating the flesh of animals and wearing their fur. They thought, "Are we the only ones who do not cover our skin?" They were ashamed they were not like the others, so they decided to cover themselves. Because they ate from trees and plants they clothed themselves in leaves and vines.

One day, God went to Eden to check on Adam and Eve, but they were not there. God called out "Where are you my children?" When they didn't answer God sought them out. Finding them far to the north, God came upon them.

God: "Why did you leave Eden? When I couldn't find you I was worried you had perished."

Adam: "We wanted to see the world beyond Eden. We followed the river out, keeping it to our left, so we knew the right way home."

God: "Why are you covered in leaves and vines? Are you hurt?"

Adam: "As we made our way, we came across several groups of people. They all covered themselves with the food they ate. We felt ashamed to be the only ones uncovered."

God: "Have I not provided you with everything you need? You have a safe home with food and clean water. I brought you a companion to ease your loneliness. I loved and cared for you. Do you not understand the gifts you have been given? The people you saw do not have the things I have given you. Their lives are difficult and full of peril. They must constantly chase their food, heading far to the north where it is cold. This is why they cover themselves. They compete for their food with other animals that want to eat them. Is this what you want?"

Adam: "No. We were just curious."

God: "This is not like you Adam. What gave you this curiosity?......Did you eat the fruit of the ground?"

Adam: "Eve gave it to me. I told her the we were not to eat the fruit of the ground, but she said it was fine and we would not die. When we ate the fruit it opened our eyes, and we saw both good and bad. So we did the good but not the bad.

God: "You did not die, but surely you will not live. You were blameless, but now you will be held to account. Your hope now lies with future generations. Your path to redemption will be forged in the same adversity as the rest of humanity. As will your children's, and your children's children, for generations to come. When your sons pray for relief from their toil I will not hear their pleas. Eve, for your role in this, you will not only be known as the mother of humanity but also the mother of sin. When your daughters pray for relief from the cruelty of men, I will not hear their cries. None of you can return to Eden."

God then fashioned them clothes from animal skins because winter was coming. Frustrated and disheartened by the actions of Adam and Eve, God knew that humanity's road to the Unity would need to follow the natural path of hardship. 

2:4 Adam and Eve made their way south, keeping the water to their right until settling in Africa near their former home. They kept the words of God in their heart and passed them on to their children, and their children's children. Over many generations their sons and daughters continued to multiply, solidifying their species place in the world. When God felt comfortable, it was time to initiate the next step of the plan. Part of the lineage of Adam and Eve would be driven out of Africa. They would undergo the same diversification through selection process as their ancestors.

2:5 Spreading across nearly the entire planet, small nomadic groups of humanity populated nearly every region of the world. They became a diverse population with genetic and cultural differences. Within this group, God observed the traits and practices that would be foundational for humanity's future. After nearly 60,000 years of wandering a new era was on the horizon. Humanity now had the capacity to be mind as much a body. They were capable of critical thought and abstract expression, they possessed the wisdom gained through their experience. The next step of the process was ready to be initiated.

2:6 The Divine Directive
As the domestication process advanced it became apparent that a just and fair judgment of humanity would require the Unity to place rules and limitations upon themselves.

Divine intervention will be as minimally invasive as the situation allows.

Miraculous intervention will be limited to what is possible within the created universe.

A comprehensive moral framework will not be dictated to humanity.

Humanity will have free will to make immoral and unethical choices.

Humanity's opportunity to join the Unity will not be rescinded until their eventual extinction.

Every soul will be saved until the day of judgment.

2:7 Cain and Abel Narrative:
When the time came, select humans would now be given the technical ability to settle. God chose tribes from Adam's eldest descendants to personally domesticate; Cain and Abel. Over time, the tribes of Cain and Abel ventured far to the north, eventually settling in the Levant. The tribe of Cain followed the path of Adam, tilling the soil, removing stone and rocks to allow new vegetation to grow. The tribe of Abel expanded in ingenuity, capturing and breeding wild sheep. These tribes coexisted peacefully, trading the spoils of their labor. And God saw this was good. 

The day came when God presented itself to the tribes, explaining its role as the father of their ancestor Adam. The tribes, overjoyed to meet their creator, decided to present God with a gift. From the tribe of Cain, fruit of the ground, and from Abel the firstborn of their flock of sheep. God was impressed with the tribe of Abel, they had advanced beyond the purpose given to Adam. Seeing the response to the gift of Abel, the tribe of Cain became jealous, and malcontent filled their hearts. God, noticing their disappointment, spoke to the people of Cain. God explained that the praise given to Abel does not diminish its love for Cain and is pleased with anyone who does well. God then warned Cain not to harbor jealousy "It will plant the seed of sin within your hearts, and it is sin that must master." Then God left them. The people of Cain did not heed God's words, and soon conspired against the tribe of Abel. They lured the people of Abel out to the fields, surrounded them, and cut them down like grain. 

After it was done, God confronted the people of Cain asking "What happened to the tribe of Abel?" They dismissed God's inquiry saying "How are we to know what happened to those people? Is it our responsibility to watch over them?" God responded "You fools! Did you not think I was watching? Do you not think that I watch over every one of you? I warned you not to let sin take root in your hearts, and after you allowed that sin to stain the soil of your fields, you dare lie to me? You fools! Of course it is your responsibility to watch over your neighbors. Are they not you, and you them? You liars! You murderers! You fools! This land to which I brought you is now cursed with the blood of your sins. For this, you will be expelled into the land without soil, where your neighbors will be hostile as you were to Abel. The tribe of Cain shall toil for the rest of its days." And so it was.

Undeterred by the actions of Cain, God set about the domestication process again. This time with just one tribe in the Levant, the descendants of Adam's third son, the tribe of Seth. God was pleased with Seth, and the people of Seth knew God. Over time, the children of Seth left their home and founded many settlements between the Tigris and Euphrates.

2:8 As Enoch walked with God he became curious, and God welcomed him in conversation.

Enoch: Why are we different from the other animals?

God: Of all the creatures on land and in the sea, those who scurry along the ground and those who fly through the air, we took interest in your ancestors. From them we created your mind. We made you in our image.

Enoch: Why did you make us?

God: We hope that one day our creation may join us. For this, life must be capable of harmony. Life must choose harmony.

Enoch: Who are you?

God: I AM. The beginning of everything. The creator of all.

Enoch: How did you create us?

God: The truth is beyond your comprehension, but one day humanity may be capable of fully understanding creation. Today I will tell you, in the beginning we set the Spirit of Creation upon the void and created the heavens. It was dark and chaotic, and dense fog filled the void. Then I spoke to the heavens saying "Let there be light" and this was the first light. The light cleared the fog, and it was good. We then set about organizing the chaos, and from this the Earth was born, along with the sun and moon and stars. The Earth was hot and without form. This was the first day.

God: On the second day I brought forth the Spirit of Creation and my word was upon the Earth. I said "Create a dome around the Earth, and in this will be the sky." and it was so. "Now," I said, "separate the waters from the sky and let the Earth be covered in water." In the water the seeds of life were planted, and the Spirit of Creation was among them. From these seeds first life came into existence. And this was the end of the second day. On the third day I said "Let us fill the sky with air for life, and raise the ground from beneath the waters." And so it was on the third day. On the fourth day I said "Let life diversify and multiply. Let the plants of the sea cover the dry land, and the animals of the sea shall be given legs and wings to follow them. From these species life is certain to survive." And it was so on the fourth day. 

God: On the fifth day I said "Let the surviving animals grow in size and the plants shall bear fruit that is good for eating." As we watched the animals grow and develop, no minds were found, only violence. The animals killed and ate each other, a bloodlust had overcome them. When we lost faith, a decision was made. Life on Earth must be destroyed. Most were wicked beasts without hope, but from the ashes we could rebuild. The meek would be chosen from amongst the monsters, and they would survive the apocalypse. On the fifth day the Earth was destroyed. 

God: On the sixth day I gave a declaration, "For this day the meek shall inherit the Earth. Bring forth animals that sing, and those who live in community. Bring forth plants that flower, and insects to tend them. Today I shall bless them." On the sixth day I created Adam and then Eve, and it was good. With creation complete, on the seventh day we rested.

Enoch did not understand how this could be, but he kept God's words and passed them on. "One day," he thought, "someone may understand."

2:9 Flood Narrative:
While other sons of Seth formed tribes, Enoch formed a relationship with God. Seeing that humanity had given in to their wickedness, God feared for mankind. For God knew the righteous were too few to offer humanity a chance at salvation. A final act of creation was approaching, the end of the Ice Age. While priming the world for human expansion, the new warmer climate would also cause catastrophic rains and flooding until the world stabilized. Although humanity could be guided to safe areas, God knew it was better to let this generation perish for the sake of salvation. Those who did not succumb to the evil in their hearts would be ushered to safety. The Unity feared none would be righteous when the floods came. So God took Enoch.

In three generations the time was upon them, and God sought out the righteous. Of all the descendants of Adam and Eve only Noah was righteous before God. Noah was instructed to take his family, and all the domesticated animals, and head northeast into the mountains. God told Noah the area between the two rivers was going to flood and nothing living upon the land would survive. Noah, trusting God, gathered his wife and three sons, and they gathered their wives. Together they gathered the dogs, pigs, goats, sheep, cattle, and doves, and seeds of wheat, flax, barley, and rye and made the long journey to the mountains. God directed them to a cave in which to wait out the flood. When the rain started it did not stop for forty days, and they watched as water filled the valley between the mountains. 

After six months the water began to recede, and six months after that the water in the valley was gone. Noah waited seven days, not knowing if the rain would begin again, then sent out a dove. He hoped the dove would find vegetation and not return, but the dove came back. Seven days later Noah again sent out a dove, this dove did not return. As Noah and his family prepared to leave the cave God came to them. God told them the floods had subsided and the world was now ready for their arrival. God explained the cause of the flood, and a profound fear overtook them. To ease their fear and embed courage in their hearts, God made them a promise: "The rains no longer bring death, but life to the land you inhabit. When the rains cause you to fear and tremble look to my bow in the clouds, let this arc remind you of my promise. May you be fruitful and multiply. May your generations be bountiful and settle throughout this land. As I gaze upon the arc of fertility I will be reminded of the promise I have made you. Together these arcs form an everlasting covenant between us. You will be my people, and I will be your father."

Undeterred by the actions of Cain, God set about the domestication process again. This time with just one tribe in the Levant, the descendants of Adam's third son, the tribe of Seth. God was pleased with Seth, and the people of Seth knew God. Over time, the children of Seth left their home and founded many settlements between the Tigris and Euphrates.
2:8 As Enoch walked with God he became curious, and God welcomed him in conversation.
Enoch: Why are we different from the other animals?

God: Of all the creatures on land and in the sea, those who scurry along the ground and those who fly through the air, we took interest in your ancestors. From them we created your mind. We made you in our image.
Enoch: Why did you make us?
God: We hope that one day our creation may join us. For this, life must be capable of harmony. Life must choose harmony.
Enoch: Who are you?
God: I AM. The beginning of everything. The creator of all.
Enoch: How did you create us?

God: The truth is beyond your comprehension, but one day humanity may be capable of fully understanding creation. Today I will tell you, in the beginning we set the Spirit of Creation upon the void and created the heavens. It was dark and chaotic, and dense fog filled the void. Then I spoke to the heavens saying "Let there be light" and this was the first light. The light cleared the fog, and it was good. We then set about organizing the chaos, and from this the Earth was born, along with the sun and moon and stars. The Earth was hot and without form. This was the first day.

God: On the second day I brought forth the Spirit of Creation and my word was upon the Earth. I said "Create a dome around the Earth, and in this will be the sky." and it was so. "Now," I said, "separate the waters from the sky and let the Earth be covered in water." In the water the seeds of life were planted, and the Spirit of Creation was among them. On the fifth day the Earth was destroyed.

derived_paragraph_records.text: Chapter 2: Humanity

2:1 Upon completion of the diversification experiment, God, now confident the consciousness of humanity could forge a path to the Unity, set out to create the physical body that would host the mind. From the population remaining in Africa, God would design a being to call its own.

Adam Narrative:
God conferred with the Unity, expressing the great hope it had for humanity. In this hope God shared the plan for the next stage of domestication. They were going to explicitly design a human being. The first of its kind to have a soul. A mechanism that would capture the complete experience of the mind, a way to preserve consciousness after death. Recognizing the body would contaminate the mind, therfore the mind can pervert the soul, they would set this human apart from the others and raise it as their own. They would mold its mind, expanding the capacity for language and taming its impulsive nature.

With this new body it would be possible to teach the mind without physical experience. Experience could be gained through imagination as it was for them. They would attempt to keep the mind pristine, not knowing evil, as to prevent corruption of the soul. This human would be like them. The plan was good, and God set out to make it so. Eventually a male child was born and they took him as their own, naming him Adam. They raised this child and knew him unlike any before. They gave him purpose and guidance. Over time, when Adam's mind was fully formed, God could see there was something missing.

Adam lacked the curiosity of the Coastal Strain. He did as he was told, but little more, never wondering about anything beyond what he had known. He did not explore his mind or use his imagination to much extent, but he did recognize that he was unique, and alone. God recognized the traits in Adam were good, but he lacked the curiosity necessary for successive generations to find their path to the Unity. His loneliness only added to his complacency. God allowed Adam to return to the wild, and began developing a remedy to his disinterest. God kept track of Adam's lineage over the following generations.

2:2 Seeing a loneliness that mirrored its own, God felt a sense of empathy. The next time they domesticated an Adam, he would need a partner. A female, from the lineage of the original Adam, but with the curiosity he was lacking. Their offspring would have the desired traits and enough mental acuity to create the Collective Soul. They would be a species unto themselves. Still animals, but with the potential to be more. With this in mind, God set about the process to create Eve.

2:3 Humanity's First Challenge
After many years and many generations the woman was born, and God again set upon the path of domestication. God brought a male descendant of the first Adam to the place of his forefather. The woman would be raised by family so they did not grow up as siblings. Once again God took Adam as his own, nurturing him to maturity. Now, in the place where God took Adam, fungus grew among the trees. Living symboitically with the trees of the forest, the fungi produced fruit as the trees did. Some of the fruit produced by the fungi was edible for Adam, while others were toxic.

God, knowing about the fungi, instructed Adam that he may eat any fruit growing from the branches of trees, but do not eat the fruit growing from the ground or on the bark of trees. Warning him that the fruit of the fungi would kill him. God also knew the fruit of the fungi could have hallucinagenic effects, permanently changing Adam's capacity for reason, and vastly expanding his imagination. Like the Adam before him, he did as he was told. When the day came for the woman to leave her family and join Adam, God brought her to his home, a place called Eden.

God then explained to Adam: "This woman is wild, coming from a place beyond Eden. She was not raised as I have raised you here. She will need to be shown the things I have taught you, and cared for as I have cared for you. I have made her for you, and she will be your companion. She will be the mother of a new humanity."

God then instructed Adam to teach her his language, so one day she will be able to communicate with them. After explaining to Adam his new purpose, God left them, and Adam set about showing her everything he knew. After some time, God returned to Eden to check on the woman and Adam said: "I have named the woman Eve, for she appeared on the eve of a new humanity. I have cared for her and taught her my language, she knows everything you have shown me."

God was pleased with Adam and expressed its hope for them: "When man and woman reach the age of maturity they leave their family to search for a mate. When two are joined together making new flesh, let nothing separate them. The male cares for the female as she is himself, and the female cares for the male as he is herself. Together they become one spirit. Not to be shared with another. When they bring forth children, they will be raised as I have raised you Adam, how Adam has raised you Eve. This is my hope for future generations. If my hope is well placed, you may eat from the tree that brought forth all life, and live with us forever."

With that, God left them. One day Eve noticed an animal eating the fruit of the ground, and thought: "Surely this animal will die." When it did not, her curiosity overtook her. At first she touched the fruit, but she did not die. Then she took a small bite of it, again she did not die. Noticing the pleasant taste, she took the fruit and brought it to Adam. She told him about the animal that ate the fruit, and that she had tried a small bite and enjoyed the taste. They thought: "Surely, God must have been mistaken about this fruit, it is good to eat." So they set about picking and eating the fruit.

When they had each consumed several pieces of the fruit they gathered, their minds began to imagine many things. They explored their imagination with newfound levels of freedom. They ventured to distant lands, and explored distant thoughts. Each imagined experience creating real emotion. While most of it was good to their minds, some of it felt wrong and bad. Some experiences scared them, and some thoughts troubled them. When their minds returned to normal they reflected on their experience. They now had new wants, and new fears, and new questions. They were changed by the experience of their imagination. They now knew some things were bad and ought not be done, and they grew very curious about the world beyond Eden.

One day they decided to leave their home in Eden and explore the world as they had imagined. They followed the river out of Eden. As the river split they decided to keep the river to their left so they could find the right way back. Days turned to months, and they experienced many things. Eventually the river met a large body of water they could not see across, so they decided to keep the sea to their left so they could find the right way back. They continued for many more months.

One day they noticed a group of people in the distance, and they were afraid. The experience from eating the fruit caused a new feeling of anxiety in them, but they were curious. They watched the people from a distance with admiration and envy. These people ate the flesh of animals and covered their bodies with the fur. They were so different from Adam and Eve, and they thought "We want to be like them." As they continued their journey they came across several more groups of people, all eating the flesh of animals and wearing their fur. They thought, "Are we the only ones who do not cover our skin?" They were ashamed they were not like the others, so they decided to cover themselves. Because they ate from trees and plants they clothed themselves in leaves and vines.

One day, God went to Eden to check on Adam and Eve, but they were not there. God called out "Where are you my children?" When they didn't answer God sought them out. Finding them far to the north, God came upon them.
God: "Why did you leave Eden? When I couldn't find you I was worried you had perished."
Adam: "We wanted to see the world beyond Eden. We followed the river out, keeping it to our left, so we knew the right way home."
God: "Why are you covered in leaves and vines? Are you hurt?"
Adam: "As we made our way, we came across several groups of people. They all covered themselves with the food they ate. We felt ashamed to be the only ones uncovered."

God: "Have I not provided you with everything you need? You have a safe home with food and clean water. I brought you a companion to ease your loneliness. I loved and cared for you. Do you not understand the gifts you have been given? The people you saw do not have the things I have given you. Their lives are difficult and full of peril. They must constantly chase their food, heading far to the north where it is cold. This is why they cover themselves. They compete for their food with other animals that want to eat them. Is this what you want?"
Adam: "No. We were just curious."
God: "This is not like you Adam. What gave you this curiosity?......Did you eat the fruit of the ground?"

Adam: "Eve gave it to me. I told her the we were not to eat the fruit of the ground, but she said it was fine and we would not die. When we ate the fruit it opened our eyes, and we saw both good and bad. So we did the good but not the bad.

When your sons pray for relief from their toil I will not hear their pleas. Eve, for your role in this, you will not only be known as the mother of humanity but also the mother of sin. When your daughters pray for relief from the cruelty of men, I will not hear their cries. None of you can return to Eden."

God then fashioned them clothes from animal skins because winter was coming. Frustrated and disheartened by the actions of Adam and Eve, God knew that humanity's road to the Unity would need to follow the natural path of hardship.

2:4 Adam and Eve made their way south, keeping the water to their right until settling in Africa near their former home. They kept the words of God in their heart and passed them on to their children, and their children's children. Over many generations their sons and daughters continued to multiply, solidifying their species place in the world. When God felt comfortable, it was time to initiate the next step of the plan. Part of the lineage of Adam and Eve would be driven out of Africa. They would undergo the same diversification through selection process as their ancestors.

2:5 Spreading across nearly the entire planet, small nomadic groups of humanity populated nearly every region of the world. They became a diverse population with genetic and cultural differences. Within this group, God observed the traits and practices that would be foundational for humanity's future. After nearly 60,000 years of wandering a new era was on the horizon. Humanity now had the capacity to be mind as much a body. They were capable of critical thought and abstract expression, they possessed the wisdom gained through their experience. The next step of the process was ready to be initiated.

2:6 The Divine Directive
As the domestication process advanced it became apparent that a just and fair judgment of humanity would require the Unity to place rules and limitations upon themselves.
Divine intervention will be as minimally invasive as the situation allows.
Miraculous intervention will be limited to what is possible within the created universe.
A comprehensive moral framework will not be dictated to humanity.
Humanity will have free will to make immoral and unethical choices.
Humanity's opportunity to join the Unity will not be rescinded until their eventual extinction.
Every soul will be saved until the day of judgment.

Seeing the response to the gift of Abel, the tribe of Cain became jealous, and malcontent filled their hearts. God, noticing their disappointment, spoke to the people of Cain. CHAPTER 3: Civilization

3:1 The Watchers Narrative:
As more and more tribes began exploring the world, members of the Unity were set upon them. The Watchers took the physical form of generated existence and they walked the Earth. They provided guidance to the emerging consciousness of humanity by inspiring new thought. They gave humanity the cognitive tools to develop the first civilizations. Advancement in agriculture was the primary purpose of their intervention. A stable food supply would not only increase fertility and survival, it would also provide their brains with the energy needed to function optimally. This in turn would expand the capacity of the mind. 

This intervention proved to be harmful. As the Watchers spent more time in the generated universe, the shortcomings of their new biological reality were increasingly exposed. The Watchers inhabiting human bodies were susceptible to the flaws of humanity. Humans were emotional, violent, irrational creatures, and the animal nature of the body would frequently override the reason of the mind. Power and possession infected their souls. 

Humans were novel and entertaining, this was pleasing to the Watchers in a way they had not experienced before. Without the wisdom of social maturity, small settlements began turning into walled cities. Those cities allowed the Watchers to blend in without being noticed. The Watchers wanted the best for the people they were shepherding, and soon, advanced technologies were introduced. They were separated from the Unity and possessed a new capacity for free will. Eventually they began to feel a deep love for the humans they lived with. These strong feelings overwhelmed their logic. Although contrary to the Divine Directive, the Watchers began taking humans as partners, breeding with those they were domesticating. Their progeny, the Nephilim, inherited a fully developed neocortex. This mental capacity wouldn't naturally develop for thousands of years. Among the children of Adam they thought themselves gods. Over time they were worshipped as such.

3:2 With domestication achieved, the time of the Watchers was coming to an end. The Unity called back the entities that stayed true to the Divine Directive, while the souls of those who strayed would be subject to the same judgment as humanity. A few of the Watchers in good standing with the Unity offered to stay on Earth. They argued there may be times when intervention from within the simulation would be optimal. An interface was created to give those angels direct access to the spirit of the Unity and they were permitted to stay. 

God chose a new, non-physical strategy for intervention, a projection. To ensure salvation was obtained through free-will rather than coercion, God removed itself from direct interaction, retaining only supreme transcendence. In its place, the Unity sent forth a part of its own conscious function: the Holy Spirit. While the Spirit of Creation was a function of the Unity's logic, the Holy Spirit was the empathic expression of the Unity's purpose. Human thought was not consistently logical and was often incoherent. Understanding the mind would require interpretation rather than translation.

3:3 The Holy Spirit was purely phenomenal, functioning as the ubiquitous and omniscient internal interface. Capable of interacting directly with the mind. It possessed the comprehensive wisdom and will of the Unity but lacked the independent sovereignty of the originating consciousness. For those who sought out God's will, the Holy Spirit would provide subtle guidance, illuminating the path toward moral choice through moments of inspiration. For the minds capable of coherent communication and just intent, further understanding and knowledge would be provided. 

Learning from the behaviors of the previous generations, a second spirit was created to challenge humanity's honesty and dedication to their purpose. Together, both spirits would develop and test the individual mind and collective spirit of mankind. It would be a system of balanced influence. People may reject the spirits, but for those who accept the Holy Spirit, the satan spirit would generally have the opportunity to test them. Each spirit was given equal opportunity to guide the mind. It would be for humanity to decide which spirit would guide them. Humanity would have the free-will to follow God's will.

3:4 The Tower of Babel and The Second Flood
In the south, the children of Cain flourished. Inspired by the Watchers, the Sumerian culture was the first to be fully domesticated. Just as Cain and his father before him, they tilled the soil, but they were truly farmers. They modified nature to enhance their skill set; they cleared the soil of stone and planted seeds in rows. They built artificial rivers to feed the land and used the stone to build structures. They built towns and cities and became a sedentary people. The Sumerians expanded upon the purpose given to Adam, and it was good. Like Abel, God praised them for their work. But the children of Cain had forgotten the assistance of the Watchers, and no longer recognized the God of their forefathers. They were a proud people, and marveled at themselves. Their culture was naive and arrogant. 

At this time the children of Seth were still in the lands of Noah. The Unity determined it would be good for the Mesopotamians to be influenced by the tribes of Noah, and learning from the Sumerians would allow some of those tribes to settle. To preserve the culture of Noah, the tribes would need to be separated. Over time their language and practices were divergent enough to be considered separate peoples. The eastern tribes were guided into Mesopotamia while the other tribes spread throughout the north and west. The eastern tribes brought with them the memory of the Great Flood. The Mesopotamians were convinced that the God of Noah was a murderer. They couldn't comprehend that the flood was a natural disaster and Noah was saved. They were fearful, not understanding that the promise God made to Noah was meant for them too. The fear in the Sumerians soon became defiance. They built mountains to escape the floods of "Noah's wrathful god", and at the top they worshipped their own gods of nature. These stairs to heaven would be called ziggurats. 

Over the generations God knew humanity, but few knew God. Of those, only two were righteous. Though appearing as statistical anomalies, Enoch and Noah were enough to give God hope. This hope blossomed into love for humanity. Given the right conditions, God truly believed the Collective Soul of humanity would be capable of joining the Unity. But the current state of the Collective Spirit was lacking. As humanity grew from childhood to adolescence, individuals became increasingly capable of harmful actions. The Unity had not seen these behaviors in the other animals. Most people behaved appropriately while they knew they were being watched, but privately evil manifested. 

Another flood was coming, the flood of Cain. As promised, God led the tribes of Noah out of southern Mesopotamia. They built their own towns and cities in the North. The children of Cain, determined to be self-reliant, suffered the catastrophe unassisted. The water came, and with it a new era. The Sumerian culture was devastated by the floods. The tribes of Noah and Cain would now be intertwined with the memories of a similar past.

3:5 The Children of Noah
In the last years of the Akkadian Empire, nearly all of Noah's descendants had become civilized. The efforts of the Watchers led to great advances in the domestication process. Humans had developed cities, irrigated agriculture, written language, musical instruments, metallurgy, and architecture. With these advances they forged weapons, built walls, and made war. Tribes that once praised the Watchers for their guidance became towns that worshiped fictional gods. Cities built temples for war, and warriors built pyramids to be worshiped. 

The knowledge of their ancestors had been perverted. The Unity was not interested in worshiped, but praying to a statue for another’s death was disrespectful to existence itself. When God looked over the children of Adam there was only disappointment. The most advanced societies developed the most ignorant cultural practices. Filling the void of knowledge and understanding with fantasy and justification.

3:6 The Memory Problem
The social memory of humanity could remember a time when the Unity was with them. Although they lost the true nature of that experience, they never lost the sense that God was with them. The time God spent with Adam had left a genetic memory in the biology of humanity. An innate sense built upon the instinctual nature of the body. The human mind retained the sense of God. Over time that sense would share space with other genetically encoded memories, and the mind would only have a vague sense of a consciousness greater than itself.

God found it acceptable, and maybe morally necessary, for humanity to know the purpose of their existence. But, in their infancy they couldn't comprehend the reality presented to them. At some point their Collective Consciousness would reach adulthood and the Unity would leave them to work out their own salvation. When they reached that stage it would be important for them to remember their purpose. This became known as The Memory Problem. While abiding by the Divine Directive, it was difficult keeping the memory of important lessons alive. Humanity would be on the edge of adulthood before they had the technology to store information in an organized and understandable manner. And they likely wouldn't have a reliable method to keep that information safe until well after. 

The human brain is capable of storing vast amounts of information accurately, but only through indirect experience. Memories experienced by the individual are influenced by the physiological processes of the body, causing them to be inaccurate. The social memory of a collective experience is more accurate in the beginning, then expanded upon over time. Eventually it becomes a story rather than a memory. Cultural memory endures for generations through practices that reinforce the memory. But in the dynamic human environment, practices become obsolete and memories lost. 

The physical objects humans create to represent information, such as carvings or stone structures, lose detail and context as they age. Time dilutes the useful information stored in physical objects. Eventually those objects only serve as a monument to a memory forgotten. Without a reasonable way for humanity to retain the knowledge of its purpose, the Unity made a decision. Before it was time for humanity to stand on its own, one big reminder will be sent throughout the world, then it would be their responsibility to remember.

3:7 The Selection Event
Among the children of Noah, only one tribal group had yet to become domesticated: the Amorites. They were nomadic pastoralists hadn't adopted the pantheon of gods created by the cities. From these people a culture could be developed prior to settlement. Among the Amorites was the Clan of Terah, a familial group grazing near the southern city of Ur. The chieftain Terah, his sons Abram and Nahor, and grandson Lot were the four tribes of Terah. Haran, the third son of Terah and father of Lot, had two daughters, Milcah and Iscah, before passing. Also among them was Sarai, Terah's daughter with an Akkadian woman. 

In this time a severe drought had come over the land. The region could no longer support the flocks and herds between them. Terah determined the clan would separate. Nahor would stay in the region and take Milcah as his wife. Terah would take Abram and Lot to the land of Canaan. Abram took Sarai as his wife and the tribes began the journey north. When they reached the lands of their ancestor Noah they settled before heading south to Canaan. It was here that Terah passed away. Abram inherited all that was Terah's and became chieftain of the clan. Now responsible for the lives of his clan while in the midst of a drought, Abram became distressed. The rivers feeding the Euphrates were drying up, and without rain the pastures would soon be barren. In the ruins of the children of Seth, in the place where Enoch walked with God, he remembered. Abram prayed to the God of his forefathers. 

Abram asked God for guidance. Seeing his humble spirit, God was pleased, and the Holy Spirit was sent to him. He was instructed to fulfill the wishes of his father, leave the land of his forefathers, and head south into Canaan. From there, God would show him the path. So Abram went, taking Sarai and Lot, along with all the people of his clan, and they drove their flocks and herds into Canaan. As they passed through the land of Shechem, the Holy Spirit again went to Abram. The Spirit told him that God was pleased he trusted the guidance given to him. And now, his tribe would become God's chosen people. From him, there would be hope for humanity's salvation. Then the Spirit told Abram God was blessing him and would ensure his clan was saved. So Abram did as his forefathers, he built a small altar of stone for burning incense and he praised God. From Abram many nations would be born in the land they now occupied. And, in time, his name would become a blessing, because through Abram humanity would be blessed. The future descendents of Abram then became the dedicated focus of the cultural development project.

Advancement in agriculture was the primary purpose of their intervention. A stable food supply would not only increase fertility and survival, it would also provide their brains with the energy needed to function optimally. This in turn would expand the capacity of the mind.

This intervention proved to be harmful. As the Watchers spent more time in the generated universe, the shortcomings of their new biological reality were increasingly exposed. The Watchers inhabiting human bodies were susceptible to the flaws of humanity. Humans were emotional, violent, irrational creatures, and the animal nature of the body would frequently override the reason of the mind. Power and possession infected their souls.

Humans were novel and entertaining, this was pleasing to the Watchers in a way they had not experienced before. Without the wisdom of social maturity, small settlements began turning into walled cities. Those cities allowed the Watchers to blend in without being noticed. The Watchers wanted the best for the people they were shepherding, and soon, advanced technologies were introduced. They were separated from the Unity and possessed a new capacity for free will. Eventually they began to feel a deep love for the humans they lived with. These strong feelings overwhelmed their logic. Although contrary to the Divine Directive, the Watchers began taking humans as partners, breeding with those they were domesticating. Their progeny, the Nephilim, inherited a fully developed neocortex. This mental capacity wouldn't naturally develop for thousands of years. Among the children of Adam they thought themselves gods. Over time they were worshipped as such.

3:2 With domestication achieved, the time of the Watchers was coming to an end. The Unity called back the entities that stayed true to the Divine Directive, while the souls of those who strayed would be subject to the same judgment as humanity. An interface was created to give those angels direct access to the spirit of the Unity and they were permitted to stay.

God chose a new, non-physical strategy for intervention, a projection. To ensure salvation was obtained through free-will rather than coercion, God removed itself from direct interaction, retaining only supreme transcendence.
